title: Puddle Jumping & Waterproofs
strapline: There's no bad weather, only the wrong clothes — so we suit up and go and jump in every puddle we can find.
intent: Children experience the pure, whole-body joy of jumping in puddles — an all-weather right, not a fair-weather treat.
Children develop gross-motor power, balance and coordination through jumping, stamping and splashing.
Children explore water, cause and effect and forces — the bigger the jump, the bigger the splash.
Children build resilience and independence dressing for the weather, and learn their bodies can handle rain.
Children learn that being outdoors in all weathers is normal, healthy and brilliant.
implementation: Kit up properly: a supply of waterproofs, wellies and warm layers so no child sits out, and support children to dress themselves.
Go out in the rain on purpose — reframe wet weather as an invitation, not a cancellation.
Let the jumping be big and free — this is whole-body play, so give space and expect splashes.
Feed in the wondering: 'what makes the biggest splash? where does the water go? which puddle is deepest?'
Add tools for extending the play — sticks to measure depth, cups to bail and pour, boats to float, a stick to trace where water flows.
Sort the practicals — a drying routine, spare socks, warm-up afterwards — so the fun isn't cut short by cold or damp.
key_questions: How can you make the biggest splash?
Which puddle do you think is the deepest?
Where do you think the rainwater goes?
Can you get your own wellies and waterproofs on?
What happens to the puddle if we all jump at once?

impact.text: Children jump, stamp, balance and negotiate space with power and control.
Children explore water, forces and cause and effect through play.
Children notice weather and seasons and what they mean for us — coats, puddles, wellies.
Children help dress themselves — wellies, waterproofs — with growing independence.
Children move every day because it feels good, whatever the weather.

enhancements: A puddle-depth challenge with marked sticks — which is the deepest today?
Bailing and pouring play — cups, jugs and guttering to move the puddle water about.
Floating boats, leaves and petals and racing them across the biggest puddle.
Tracing where the water runs and pools, following it with sticks and chalk on dry patches.
A rainy-day 'welly wall' hook and drying routine so the kit is always ready to go.

playing_exploring: Children throw themselves into joyful, whole-body water play whatever the weather.
Puddles invite open exploration — splashing, pouring, measuring, floating.
active_learning: The sheer fun keeps children engaged and returning to the puddles again and again.
Dressing themselves and braving the rain builds real independence and resilience.
creating_thinking: Children predict and test what makes the biggest splash or where water flows.
They reason about depth, cause and effect and the movement of water.
